solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Execute composition of Elgar thus

indicators.note: a composition puts its material together in a new order, so the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to perform a piece by Elgar in the following way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Execute' reads like playing music, but it means to kill; 'composition of' shuffles ELGAR and THUS.
explanation.definitionFit: To slaughter people or animals is to kill them, which is what execute means as a verb.

clue.text: Climbing mountains tricky at first. Don't fall like this!

indicators.note: in a down answer climbing runs upward, so the mountains are read backwards

parts.note: the Alps are mountains

indicators.note: picks the opening letter of the word tricky

explanation.surface: A climber's warning on a difficult mountain: watch you don't plunge down.
explanation.definitionFit: The noise of hitting the ground hard is a splat, the way not to fall.

clue.text: Criminals first to feed penniless priests

indicators.note: feeding puts something inside, so one piece goes into the other
penniless means without a penny, P, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: parsons are priests
first is written 1ST, read as IST

explanation.surface: Lawbreakers are the first to give food to poor clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penniless' takes P (penny) out of PARSONS, leaving ARSONS.
explanation.definitionFit: People who set fire to property deliberately are committing a crime, so they are criminals.

clue.text: Poke Chuck in bottom. His company's not wanted

indicators.note: in a down answer the bottom is the lower part, so the musician goes below

parts.note: to goose someone is to poke them, usually in the backside
Chuck Berry was the American rock and roll musician

explanation.surface: Jab Chuck in the backside; nobody wants him around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in bottom' seems to belong with 'Poke', but it places BERRY at the foot of the entry. A gooseberry is British slang for a third person spoiling a couple's time alone.
explanation.definitionFit: In British idiom, the unwanted third person with a courting couple is said to play the gooseberry.

clue.text: Objection about Brie — unfortunately it makes you fatter

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the objection is read backwards

parts.note: but, as in no ifs or buts, is an objection

indicators.note: something going unfortunately goes wrong, so the cheese's letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone objects to Brie because it is fattening.
explanation.definitionFit: Tubbier means more plump or rounder, a comparative synonym for heavier in build.

clue.text: Parisian to be held by snitch in hideout

indicators.note: being held by something means sitting inside it, so the French goes within

parts.note: a rat is an informer or snitch
être is French for to be

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is about to be captured by an informer in his hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a quiet, secluded place to withdraw to, like a hideaway.

clue.text: Beastly African in post office

parts.note: in, meaning fashionable, can be hip

explanation.surface: Someone animal-like from Africa is found working at a post office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a placement word but is the slang sense of fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: The hippopotamus is a large beast native to Africa, so a beastly African is one.

clue.text: Religious theory regularly baffles novice

indicators.note: a baffle is a screen placed in the way, so the novice is set inside
regularly picks every other letter of theory

parts.note: L, for learner, is a novice

explanation.surface: A theory about faith often confuses a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: Something holy is sacred or devout, which is what religious can mean.

clue.text: She's right to wear ring

definitions.note: she is, a girl's name; the 's is is

indicators.note: the ring is worn around the R, so that letter goes inside

parts.note: a peal is a ring of bells

explanation.surface: A woman is entitled to put on a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests jewellery; the ring is a ring of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name is what she is, and this one is an English female first name.

clue.text: Frank finished with no definite conclusion

parts.note: frank means candid or open
finished is ended

explanation.surface: Frank has finished but nothing has been settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name but means candid.
explanation.definitionFit: A question left without a fixed limit or answer has no settled outcome, so it has no definite conclusion.

clue.text: Catch girl with nothing on

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece on another follows it, so the zero goes after the girl

parts.note: a lass is a girl
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: An instruction to grab a young woman who is naked.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a rope used to catch cattle, and as a verb it means to catch with one.

clue.text: Fierce old woman fighting against sack

indicators.note: against here means placed right up next to, so the second piece is set beside the first

parts.note: fighting is battle
to sack someone is to give them the axe

explanation.surface: An aggressive elderly woman resisting being dismissed from her job.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a formidable, aggressive older woman is a battleaxe.

clue.text: You might apply this to your cuts

definitions.text: You might apply this to your cuts

parts.words: You might apply this to your cuts
parts.note: cuts suggest wounds needing ointment, but they are cuts of meat, which a cook softens with a powder or a mallet

explanation.surface: Advice about putting antiseptic on wounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests first aid; the cuts are butcher's cuts of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A meat softener, powder or mallet, is applied to cuts of beef to make them less tough.

clue.text: Leg it with circus performer, did you say?

indicators.note: asks whether something was said, pointing to a word that sounds like another

parts.note: a flea circus has fleas as its performers

explanation.surface: Running away with a clown or acrobat, as someone asks.
explanation.definitionFit: To leg it is British slang for running away, the same as to escape quickly.

clue.text: He introduces Ron and Doris, errant wife

indicators.note: introducing someone comes first, so this word leads the answer
errant means straying, so these letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A man introduces Ron and Doris, a wayward wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her indoors' is British slang, from the TV show Minder, for a man's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is jokey British slang a husband uses for his spouse, so it names a wife.

clue.text: On reflection, regrets uncle becoming a manipulative type

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things the other way round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: rues means regrets
Uncle Sam personifies the USA; uncle gives SAM

explanation.surface: Thinking it over, someone sorry that an uncle turns into a schemer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manipulative' suggests scheming but means working the body with the hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A massage therapist manipulates muscles with the hands, so is literally a manipulative type.

clue.text: TV celebrity radiates male embarrassment

indicators.note: embarrassment throws someone into confusion, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A television celebrity's man gives off awkwardness.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous figure on television is a star of broadcasting, a famous person in the media.

clue.text: Time small boy in Scotland sang

parts.note: wee is the Scottish word for small, hence in Scotland
Ted is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A little Scottish lad is timed while singing.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds tweet when they sing, so tweeted is a past tense for chirped a song.

clue.text: What you may get if patient?

definitions.text: What you may get if patient?

parts.words: What you may get if patient?
parts.note: patient suggests the virtue of waiting, as if a reward came, but here it is the noun: someone being cared for by a doctor

explanation.surface: Asking what good things come to those who wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patient' is an adjective in the surface but the noun in the reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A person under a doctor's care receives medical care, which is what a patient gets.

clue.text: Leaves sweets for the Speaker

indicators.note: what the speaker says is heard, not seen spelt, so a word with the same sound is wanted

parts.note: sweets, in British usage, are puddings, also called desserts

explanation.surface: Someone in Parliament's Speaker's chair is left sweets or treats.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert someone is to abandon them, which is what leaves means as a verb here.

clue.text: Dishonoured bride ill-used to a degree on journey north

indicators.note: in a down answer going north runs upward, so the letters are read backwards
only to a degree means only partly, so a run of letters is taken from these words

explanation.surface: A mistreated bride, somewhat disgraced, travels northwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A sullied reputation is stained or tarnished, the same as one that has been disgraced.

clue.text: Pay saint very little money to conclude

parts.note: one penny, written 1P, is very little money, with the 1 read as I
to conclude is to end

explanation.surface: Paying a holy figure only a pittance to finish the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a regular fixed salary, especially for clergy, so it is a kind of pay.

clue.text: Hot spot where paper has revolutionary role

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the role is read backwards

parts.note: a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: A trouble zone where a newspaper takes a revolutionary line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot spot' suggests a trouble zone; it is a sheltered sunny place. The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheltered garden corner that catches sunshine and stays warm is a literal hot spot.

clue.text: Spots Bill heading north-east

indicators.note: the bill sits ahead of the direction, which follows it

parts.note: AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: A man named Bill sees something as he travels north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name but is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin condition producing pimples is what spots means as a plural noun.

clue.text: Vegan's latest pie quietly chucked out? It's horrible!

indicators.note: the latest is the final one, so the last letter of Vegan's is taken
chucked out means thrown away, so the letter for quiet is removed

parts.note: a pasty is a pastry pie
P, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A vegan throws away a pie, finding it disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of Vegan's is N (the apostrophe and s count as the word's end letters are only VEGAN).
explanation.definitionFit: Something nasty is unpleasant or vile, a direct synonym of the adjective horrible.

clue.text: Bedsit land unexpectedly provides romantic prospects

indicators.note: something happening unexpectedly comes out in a surprising form, so these letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Living in a cheap one-room flat brings surprising chances of love.
explanation.walkthrough: A bedsit is a British one-room rented flat; 'unexpectedly' rearranges BEDSIT LAND.
explanation.definitionFit: Meetings arranged between strangers are possible romances, so they are prospects of love.

clue.text: A Hereford pilot?

definitions.meaning: Hereford is a breed of beef cattle, and a castrated bull of it is one
to pilot is to guide or direct a vehicle

explanation.surface: A pilot from the English town of Hereford.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereford is an English city that gives its name to a breed of beef cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: A castrated young bull raised for beef, and the verb to guide a ship, both fit.

clue.text: Sex before church is a sin

indicators.note: one piece comes before the other in the answer

parts.note: sex is Latin for six, written VI in Roman numerals
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Sex before marriage in church is considered sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is the Latin word for six, which gives the Roman numeral VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice is an immoral habit or wrongdoing, a synonym for a sin.

clue.text: I swear, getting grumpier with F1 interruptions

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into something, so one piece goes into the middle of another

parts.note: testier means more irritable, grumpier
F1 is read as the letters F and I

explanation.surface: Someone cursing as Formula One keeps interrupting, getting more irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I swear' looks like an oath, but it is the definition: one who swears in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gives evidence under oath swears to tell the truth, so a witness says I swear.

clue.text: Fat old cow's complaint about Spain

indicators.note: about means around, so the disease's letters go round the country code

parts.note: BSE, mad cow disease, is a cattle illness
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: An elderly heavy cow is complaining about Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very overweight, the extreme sense of fat as an adjective.

clue.text: A sound agreement?

parts.note: a sound agreement suggests a solid deal, but here it is words whose sounds agree at their endings

explanation.surface: Asking whether a firm, reliable deal has been struck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective meaning reliable but means noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Words like cat and hat agree in their final sounds, so verse matching is an agreement of sound.

clue.text: I doorstep desperate bank customer

indicators.note: desperate means wild and frantic, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A frantic bank client turns up on someone's doorstep.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who puts money into an account at a bank is a person making a deposit.
